title: How to Seal Redwood: Keep It Red on Decks, Fences and Tables
description: Seal redwood in 7 steps with a redwood-toned oil, not a clear coat: clean, brighten with oxalic acid, dry 24 to 48 hours, recoat every 1 to 3 years.
dek: Seal redwood with a redwood-toned penetrating oil, not a clear: clean, brighten with oxalic acid, apply 1 thin coat and recoat every 1 to 3 years.
intro: A clear coat keeps redwood dry but lets the red fade. A lightly pigmented penetrating oil keeps both, on decks, fences, gates, railings and tables.

Seal redwood with a lightly pigmented, redwood-toned penetrating oil rather than a clear: clean it, brighten it with oxalic acid, apply one or two thin coats and recoat every one to three years. Sun and surface change the details. This guide covers new and gray redwood, decks, fences, gates, railings, tables and indoor floors.

quickAnswer: Seal redwood with a penetrating oil that carries a little redwood-toned pigment, not a clear coat. Clean the wood, brighten it with oxalic acid, let it dry for a day or two, then apply one or two thin coats and wipe off whatever the wood does not absorb. Outdoors, plan on a maintenance coat every one to three years. Indoors, where there is no sun or rain, a clear film finish such as polyurethane is fine.

blocks.p: Every step below follows the same logic as our [redwood sealer rankings](/best-redwood-sealer/): redwood is bought for its color, and the finish has one main job, which is keeping that color.

sections.h: Why Does Clear Sealer Fail So Fast on Redwood?

blocks.p: A clear sealer fails on redwood because it does almost nothing about sunlight. Redwood's red comes from extractives concentrated near the surface of the board, and ultraviolet light breaks them down within weeks of exposure. A clear finish keeps rain out, which slows checking, cupping and the dark streaks that water leaves as it leaches those extractives, but the color still drifts from red to tan and then toward gray.
That is why so many owners who search for the best clear coat for a redwood deck end up disappointed. Clear products also generally need yearly recoats on open decks.

Pigment changes the outcome. A finish tinted with transparent red or brown iron oxide blocks a share of UV at the surface, so the finish fades rather than the wood under it, and each maintenance coat restores both the protection and the color.
THE RULE
To keep redwood red, use a finish that is a little red.
Clear keeps the wood dry. A transparent redwood tone keeps it dry and keeps the color, and it evens out pale sapwood at the same time.

blocks.h3: When is a clear sealant on redwood the right choice?

blocks.p: Clear still has a place. Use it on covered porches, under deep eaves and on furniture that sits in shade, where UV is not the main threat. Use it if you like silver gray redwood. Everywhere else, a toned penetrating oil is the better buy.

sections.h: When Should You Seal New Redwood?

blocks.p: Seal new redwood as soon as it is clean, dry and absorbs water, which is often within a few weeks of installation. Redwood is normally kiln-dried or air-dried before sale, so the old advice to let a new deck weather for a full year works against you here: the first months of sun cause the fastest color loss, and waiting means sealing wood that has already faded.

Use the water drop test to decide. Sprinkle water on several boards, including the sunniest ones. If it darkens the wood and soaks in within a minute or two, the surface is open and ready. If it beads, something is blocking absorption and oil will sit on top.

blocks.h3: What is mill glaze, and how do you deal with it?

blocks.p: Mill glaze is a term owners and finish makers use for the smooth, slightly shiny surface some planed boards have when they leave the mill. There are three common fixes: let the boards weather for a few weeks until water soaks in, wash them with a deck cleaner and brightener, or scuff them with roughly 60 to 80 grit sandpaper along the grain. Many finish labels list their own new-wood preparation, so read yours first.

blocks.h3: Is one coat of oil-based semi-transparent stain over new redwood OK?

blocks.p: Yes, one coat is often all new redwood can take. Many penetrating oils call for a single coat on new wood, with any second coat applied wet on wet before the first dries. What matters is that the wood absorbs it: apply thinly, wait the time on the label, and wipe off anything still sitting on the surface. A second coat on top of a cured first coat that the wood could not absorb is the usual cause of a sticky, glossy finish that peels in patches.

sections.h: How Do You Clean and Brighten Gray Redwood Before Sealing?

blocks.p: Clean gray redwood with an oxygen-based deck cleaner, rinse it at low pressure, then neutralize and brighten it with an oxalic acid brightener before sealing. The gray is only a thin layer of weathered fibers; the red heartwood is still underneath, and this two-step prep brings much of it back.

Oxygen cleaners use sodium percarbonate to lift dirt, mildew and the gray layer without the fiber damage chlorine bleach causes. Apply it to wet wood, let it work for the labeled time and scrub along the grain with a synthetic brush. Rinse with a garden hose or a pressure washer on low pressure with a wide fan tip, held well back from the boards. Redwood is soft, and a narrow, high-pressure stream carves the earlywood and leaves a fuzzy, washboard surface that takes finish unevenly.

Cleaners are alkaline, and alkaline wood looks darker and duller. The oxalic acid brightener lowers the pH, restores much of the red and neutralizes the cleaner so the finish bonds properly. Rinse thoroughly afterward and let the wood dry, usually 24 to 48 hours of dry weather, before you seal.

blocks.h3: What causes tannin bleed and black stains on redwood?

blocks.p: Redwood is rich in tannins, and they cause two kinds of stain. The first is tannin bleed: water moving through the wood carries tannins to the surface and leaves brown streaks, most often below fasteners and where roof water drips. The second is iron staining, the blue-black spots that form when iron from steel nails, steel wool or a wire brush reacts with those tannins. Oxalic acid removes both, and a second targeted pass usually clears stubborn spots.

Prevent the iron stains from coming back by using stainless steel fasteners and hardware on visible redwood and never cleaning it with steel wool or a plain steel brush. If you paint redwood, use a stain-blocking primer, or tannins can bleed through latex as brown blotches.

Oxalic acid is toxic if swallowed and irritates skin and eyes. Wear chemical-resistant gloves and eye protection, keep children and pets away until it is rinsed off, and wet down nearby plants before and after.

sections.h: How Do You Best Seal Exterior Redwood Deck Boards?

blocks.p: Seal redwood deck boards with a redwood-toned penetrating oil, applied thinly with the grain and back-brushed, on a mild, dry day out of direct midday sun. Horizontal boards take the most sun and foot traffic, so a deck needs more pigment and more frequent attention than any other redwood on the property.

Most penetrating finishes list an application range of roughly 50 to 90 degrees and need a rain-free window afterward; check your label for its exact numbers. Work two or three full-length boards at a time and never stop mid-board. Back-brush each section to work the finish into the grain, give end grain and pale sapwood an extra pass because they drink more, and wipe up whatever the wood has not absorbed within the label's wait time.
Do railings and other vertical parts first, then the floor, working toward an exit. Mix all the cans together in one bucket first so a tinted color stays even across the deck.

blocks.h3: What's the best preservative or oil-based sealer for a redwood deck?

blocks.p: For most redwood decks, the best preservative is a pigmented penetrating oil rather than a clear water repellent or a film-forming stain. Products owners commonly use on redwood include Penofin Blue Label, Ready Seal 520 Redwood and TWP 1500 Series in its redwood tone, with Sikkens ProLuxe Cetol SRD for decks in harsh sun. Each is ranked with its tradeoffs in our [best redwood sealer guide](/best-redwood-sealer/), and the [best oil-based deck stains](/best-oil-based-deck-stain/) cover the broader category if you want to compare chemistries.
Avoid solid stains and paint on a redwood deck unless the boards are badly weathered or mismatched. A film over soft redwood tends to peel under foot traffic, and the only fix is stripping.
SAFETY
Oily rags can catch fire on their own.

Rags soaked in drying oils heat up as they cure and can ignite in a pile, in a trash can or in the back of a truck. Lay used rags flat outdoors to dry, or put them in a metal container filled with water and seal it before disposal.

sections.h: What Is the Best Stain and Sealer for a Redwood Fence or Gate?

blocks.p: The best stain for a redwood fence is a redwood-toned or semi-transparent penetrating oil that sprays evenly without lap marks. Fences are vertical, so they shed water and catch angled sun, and a toned finish lasts noticeably longer on a fence than on a deck.

Long fences are easiest to spray. Use a pump or airless sprayer, then back-brush or back-roll each section to push the finish into the grain and catch drips. Cover plants and cars, and skip breezy days. Our [fence stain rankings](/best-fence-stain/) sort products by how well they spray and how evenly they fade, which matters more on a long run than on a small deck.
Seal both faces of the fence where you can reach them, plus the tops of pickets and the bottom edges, because end grain soaks up water the fastest.

blocks.h3: What should you seal an exterior redwood gate with?

blocks.p: Seal a redwood gate with the same toned penetrating oil as the fence so the color matches, and give it more care. Take it off its hinges if you can and finish every face, edge and end, including the bottom edge, which is where gates rot first. Use stainless or hot-dip galvanized hinges and latches; plain steel hardware leaves rust and tannin streaks running down the boards.

blocks.h3: What is the best oil penetrating redwood fence stain and sealer?

blocks.p: Look for a penetrating oil sold in a redwood or cedar tone that the maker says can be sprayed. Ready Seal markets its formula as needing no back-brushing and leaving no lap marks, which suits big fences, while Penofin and TWP give more control on smaller runs. If you also have cedar on the property, our [cedar stain picks](/best-deck-stain-for-cedar/) use the same penetrating, lightly pigmented approach, so one product often covers both.

sections.h: What Product Should You Use on Outdoor Redwood Railings?

blocks.p: Use the same redwood-toned penetrating oil as the deck on outdoor redwood railings, applied thinly and wiped very well. Railings are touched every day, so a finish that stays tacky or peels shows there first, and a penetrating oil that has soaked in and cured leaves nothing to stick to hands or flake off.
Railings with balusters add a lot of surface area, so measure them separately when you buy finish. A pad or brush beats a sprayer on balusters; keep a rag handy for runs under the top rail.

The top rail of a deck takes as much sun as the floor and sheds less water, because it is flat. Check it with the water drop test each spring, and give it a light maintenance coat when water stops beading even if the balusters still look fine. Spar varnish suits only a covered handrail; in full sun owners commonly report it cracking and peeling.

sections.h: What Is the Best Redwood Table Sealer?

blocks.p: For an outdoor redwood table, the best sealer is a thin, redwood-toned penetrating oil that you wipe nearly dry and refresh once or twice a season. For an indoor redwood table, a clear film finish such as oil-based or water-based polyurethane is fine, because sun and rain are not attacking it.

blocks.p: Penetrating oils win on ease: a dirty, faded tabletop needs only a wash, a light scuff and a fresh coat, and nobody has to strip anything. Their downside is frequency. Film finishes win on wipeability and look great at first, but outdoors they eventually crack along the grain and lift, and the fix is sanding back to bare wood.

Prep a table like a deck, but scrub by hand instead of pressure washing, and sand lightly at 120 to 150 grit once dry for a smoother top. Apply oil with a rag or brush, let it soak in, and wipe the surface until it feels dry to the touch. Seal the underside and the end grain of the legs too.

If food will sit directly on the table, check the finish label for its cure time and any food-contact guidance before you use it, and when in doubt use placemats and boards. For tables, benches and other outdoor wood beyond decks, our [exterior wood sealer guide](/best-exterior-wood-sealer/) matches finishes to each project.

sections.h: How Do You Seal Redwood Flooring and Indoor Furniture?

blocks.p: Indoors, seal redwood with a clear film finish such as polyurethane, because the reasons film finishes fail outside, UV and standing water, are largely absent. On soft, easily dented redwood, a hard film is an advantage.

Oil-based polyurethane ambers as it ages, which deepens redwood's color and suits it well. Water-based polyurethane stays clearer and dries faster with less odor, but it can make redwood look slightly flatter. On floors, use a product rated for floors and follow the label's coat count and recoat times; floor finish labels commonly call for several thin coats with a light scuff sanding between them. Test on a scrap first, since tannin-rich woods can react with some water-based finishes and show blotches; a coat of dewaxed shellac as a sealer is a common way to prevent it.

A wipe-on oil gives indoor furniture a softer look but protects less against spills. Whatever you choose, work with windows open and a fan pulling air out, wear a respirator rated for organic vapors when using solvent-based products, and treat every oily rag as a fire risk.

sections.h: How Often Should You Reseal Redwood?

blocks.p: Most redwood decks need a fresh coat every one to three years, fences and siding can go longer, and outdoor tables may need a light coat every season. The water drop test decides it, not the calendar: when water soaks into the sunniest boards instead of beading, it is time.

blocks.p: These intervals are typical ranges drawn from finish labels and owner reports, not guarantees; climate sets the pace. Coastal fog slows fading but brings mildew, while desert and high-altitude sun can strip a deck's color in one summer.

Maintenance coats are easy with penetrating finishes. Clean, brighten, let the wood dry and apply a thin coat only where it is needed, such as the stairs and the path to the door; the new coat blends with the old. Do not stack coats on wood that still beads water, because the new finish cannot penetrate and sits on top, sticky and dark. Stay with the same product and tone, and write down the brand, color and date so the next coat matches.

mistakes: Using a Clear Sealer and Expecting the Red to Stay

Clear finishes keep water out but do little against UV, so redwood still fades to tan and gray, often within a season on a sunny deck. If color is the reason you bought redwood, pick a transparent redwood tone. The lightest tint in a line is usually enough to keep the boards reading as redwood.
Waiting a Year to Seal New Redwood

The first months of sun cause the fastest color loss, so letting a new deck weather for a year means sealing wood that has already faded. Once the boards are dry and a water drop soaks in within a minute or two, clean and finish them. If water beads, deal with the mill glaze first.
Blasting Redwood With a High-Pressure Washer

Redwood is soft. A narrow, high-pressure stream raises fuzz and gouges the earlywood, and the damaged surface absorbs finish unevenly and looks blotchy for years. Let the cleaner do the work, use a wide fan tip on low pressure and hold the wand back from the boards. Fuzz sands off; gouges stay.

Deck cleaners are alkaline and leave redwood darker and duller, and they do not remove the blue-black iron stains or tannin streaks. Skipping the brightener seals all of that in. An oxalic acid brightener restores much of the red, neutralizes the cleaner and helps the finish penetrate. Rinse it off thoroughly before sealing.

Oil that the wood cannot absorb stays on the surface, turns sticky, collects dirt and wears off in patches. Apply thin coats, wipe off what has not soaked in by the label's wait time, and never recoat wood that still beads water. Over-application causes more redwood finish complaints than any brand does.
bottomLine: To seal redwood well, skip the clear coat and use a lightly pigmented, redwood-toned penetrating oil. Clean gently, brighten with oxalic acid, let the wood dry, apply thin coats and wipe off the excess. Seal new redwood as soon as it absorbs water instead of waiting a year, and keep steel away from the wood. Then maintain it on the water drop test: decks every one to three years, fences and gates a little less often, outdoor tables every season or two, and indoor pieces under a clear film only when they wear. Handle oily rags as the fire risk they are, and the red will last.

faqs.q: What is the best redwood table sealer?
faqs.a: Outdoors, a thin redwood-toned penetrating oil is the best redwood table sealer for most owners: it keeps the color, never peels and renews with a quick clean and a fresh coat each season or two. Indoors, polyurethane is a good choice because there is no UV or rain to defeat it.

faqs.q: What's the best oil based sealer for redwood?
faqs.a: Penofin Blue Label, Ready Seal 520 Redwood and TWP 1500 Series in a redwood tone are oil-based finishes owners commonly use on redwood, and Cabot Australian Timber Oil gives a richer color. All are penetrating oils that fade rather than peel. Choose a redwood tone and test it on a sapwood board first.

faqs.q: Can you put a clear sealant on redwood?
faqs.a: Yes, but it will not keep the color. A clear sealant slows water damage, checking and mildew, but it blocks little UV, so redwood still fades to tan and then gray. Clear makes sense on covered porches, shaded furniture, indoor pieces, or if you like the gray look. For color retention outdoors, use a transparent redwood-toned finish instead.

faqs.q: Is one coat of oil-based semi-transparent stain enough on new redwood?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many penetrating oils call for a single coat on new boards, with any second coat applied wet on wet. The key is absorption: do the water drop test first, apply thinly and wipe off what does not soak in. Follow your product's label, since coat counts vary between brands.

faqs.q: How long after sealing redwood can you use the deck?
faqs.a: It depends on the product, temperature and humidity, so the label is the authority. Oil-based penetrating finishes generally need longer than water-based ones, and cool or damp weather stretches every dry time. Wait longer still before returning furniture and rugs.

faqs.q: Should you seal both sides of a redwood fence?
faqs.a: Yes, when you can reach them. Sealing only the street side lets the other face and the end grain soak up water, which drives tannin streaks and uneven aging. Coat both faces, the tops of the pickets and the bottom edges. If a neighbor owns the other side, ask first.

faqs.q: Does redwood need to be sealed at all?
faqs.a: Redwood heartwood resists decay naturally, so it will not rot quickly unsealed, but it will turn gray, check and grow mildew. Pale sapwood boards benefit even more. If you want redwood to stay red and smooth, it needs a toned penetrating finish and a maintenance coat every one to three years outdoors.
